title: Shiva comes home
hook: the fight; the head; Parvati's grief stops the universe

segments.voice: Yesterday, ganas, Shiva's attendants, and the boy, Parvati's son,, made from earth, with one instruction. Your line was some things need a guard. Did you guard ten minutes? Today, someone comes to the door. Day twenty-three.

Shiva has been away, and now he walks home up the mountain, to his own house. At his own door there's a boy he has never seen, holding a staff. The boy says: you can't come in. Shiva says: this is my house. The boy says: my mother said no one. Anyone. Shiva sends his ganas to move the child. The boy beats them back. More come. He beats them back too. The gods arrive to help, and in the Shiva Purana even they can't get past him. This is a house fight that has turned into a war. And then Shiva, who has never been told no at his own door, raises his trident. And the boy's head is gone.
screen: `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: Stop there for a second, because this is a hard story, and the tradition doesn't soften it. Both of them are right. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Nobody is the villain, and something terrible happens anyway. Family fights can look like that. Now Parvati comes out. And her grief is not quiet. In the Shiva Purana, she is so angry and so heartbroken that she calls up goddesses, fierce forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Heaven starts to come apart. The gods who fought the boy now come begging. The sage Narada and the gods plead with her, and she gives them her terms: bring my son back to life, and give him a place of honor among you. Otherwise, no universe. The scene turns on two things. First: grief has power. This tradition doesn't tell a mother to calm down. Her grief is so big that it stops everything, and everyone has to deal with it. Second: the one who broke it has to fix it. Shiva, the great god, now has to mend what he broke. And he agrees. That's the turn. What broke can be mended. Not unbroken. The boy will not come back the same, and tomorrow you'll see how he comes back. But mended. Shiva is often honored as the one who destroys so that things can begin again. Here, he is the one who has to help something begin again.
screen: `BOTH OF THEM ARE RIGHT.` · `HER GRIEF STOPS THE UNIVERSE.` · `THE ONE WHO BROKE IT MENDS IT.` · then, large: `WHAT BROKE CAN BE MENDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a broken thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life that broke. A friendship. A promise. Maybe something you broke yourself, without meaning to. Don't try to fix it right now. Just look at it honestly, the way Parvati refused to pretend. Then ask one question: is there a way this could be mended? Not made new. Mended. If you pray, you can hold it up to God. If you don't, just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Trident, the weapon Shiva raised at his own door. The fight that followed, and Parvati's grief, strong enough that the gods agree to mend what they broke.
Your line: what broke can be mended. Today, take one small step toward mending something: a text, an apology, a glue bottle. Day twenty-three.

howItsDone: Hindus tell this story as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi, carrying both the weight of Parvati's grief and the mending that follows.

original.note: Sanskrit: three spears, the trident Shiva carries.

trapdoor: what you thought: a god loses his temper and that's the story.
what it means: two people both in the right, a terrible mistake, and a grief big enough that the one who broke it has to mend it.
what a scholar hears: in the Shiva Purana, Parvati sends out fierce shaktis, forms of her own power; the goddess's anger is a real force in this tradition, not a mood.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda (the battle at the door and Parvati's anger)
